entities.name: Niels Bohr
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Niels Henrik David Bohr (1885–1962) was a Danish physicist who fundamentally reshaped our understanding of atomic structure and quantum mechanics. His 1913 model of the atom—with electrons orbiting the nucleus in quantised energy levels—earned him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922 and launched the quantum revolution that defines modern physics.

Bohr's atomic model solved the mystery of why atoms emit light at specific frequencies by applying Planck's quantum theory to Rutherford's nuclear model. He showed that electrons occupy discrete orbits and emit photons when jumping between them—a breakthrough that explained the entire periodic table of elements.

At his Institute for Theoretical Physics in Copenhagen (founded 1921), Bohr mentored a generation of physicists—Heisenberg, Pauli, Dirac, and Landau among them. The 'Copenhagen interpretation' of quantum mechanics, developed there, remains the standard framework for understanding quantum phenomena. His principle of complementarity (wave-particle duality) challenged classical logic itself.

During World War II, Bohr escaped Nazi-occupied Denmark to Sweden in a fishing boat and joined the Allied atomic research effort. He later advocated for peaceful use of nuclear energy and international arms control. His conversations with Heisenberg in occupied Copenhagen (1941) remain among modern science's most debated episodes.
